1.title: Appropriate Use, Data Sensitivity and Privacy
1.text: Welcome to Module thirteen: Appropriate Use, Data Sensitivity and Privacy. This module covers appropriate use, data sensitivity and privacy. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Which uses of Claude are appropriate, need extra controls, or are not allowed. How to classify data and decide what may go into Claude. How to protect privacy: minimize, anonymize, use approved tools and settings. What regulation means for everyday use.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Three Requests
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Three Requests. Marketing wants Claude to draft a spring campaign. H R wants Claude to rank candidates and send rejections. Finance wants Claude to check a file of raw payment-card details for errors. The first is fine; the second needs a person to decide; the third should not happen as asked.

1.title: Appropriate and Inappropriate Use Cases
1.text: Appropriate and Inappropriate Use Cases. The figure shows this: Use cases fall into three zones: appropriate, allowed with controls and human review, and not allowed.

1.title: Appropriate and Inappropriate Use Cases, continued
1.text: Appropriate and Inappropriate Use Cases, continued. Appropriate. Examples: Drafting, summarizing public or non-sensitive material, brainstorming, formatting, learning, planning. What to do: Use normally; still check accuracy. Allowed with controls. Examples: High-risk areas: legal, medical, financial, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education, public benefits; any work with personal or confidential data. What to do: Qualified human reviews before delivery or action; tell affected people A I was involved; follow policy; minimize data.

1.title: Appropriate and Inappropriate Use Cases, continued
1.text: Appropriate and Inappropriate Use Cases, continued. Not allowed. Examples: Anything that breaks the law or Anthropic's Usage Policy: fraud, phishing, harassment, disinformation, fake reviews, unauthorized access, weapons, sexually explicit content, surveillance or tracking people without consent, misuse of others' private data. What to do: Do not do it; report concerns to your policy owner. The Usage Policy also covers deception: artificial activity (sockpuppets, astroturfing, fake reviews), impersonation, and false election or medical claims. High-risk decisions about people need a human who can change the result; Claude's output is advice, not the decision. Consumer-facing chatbots must make clear that the user is dealing with A I.

1.title: Appropriate and Inappropriate Use Cases, continued
1.text: Appropriate and Inappropriate Use Cases, continued. Ask: Is the purpose lawful and ethical? Is the data allowed? What if the output is wrong? Who is accountable? Exam tip: Sort scenarios into the three zones. Legal, medical, hiring, credit and similar decisions are allowed only with qualified human review and disclosure; deception and unauthorized access are not allowed.

1.title: Data Sensitivity
1.text: Data Sensitivity. The figure shows this: A traffic-light view of data sensitivity: public is fine, internal needs the approved tool, confidential and regulated data needs policy approval or must be removed.

1.title: Data Sensitivity, continued
1.text: Data Sensitivity, continued. Public. Examples: Published catalog, press releases. Rule of thumb: Fine to use. Internal. Examples: Draft plans, internal procedures, non-sensitive metrics. Rule of thumb: Use with approved tools and accounts per policy. Confidential. Examples: Contracts, unreleased products, pricing strategy, source code, trade secrets. Rule of thumb: Only if policy permits and the tool and plan are approved; limit scope. Regulated or sensitive. Examples: Personal data (P I I): names with account numbers, addresses, I Ds; health data (P H I); payment card data; financial account numbers; children's data; credentials and passwords. Rule of thumb: Do not paste unless policy and the contract explicitly allow it; otherwise remove or anonymize.

1.title: Data Sensitivity, continued
1.text: Data Sensitivity, continued. Principles. Data minimization: share only what the task needs. Anonymize or redact identifiers before upload (replace names with I Ds like "Customer seventeen"; remove account numbers, emails, phone numbers). Never put passwords, keys or secrets in prompts, Projects, skills or artifacts. Follow your organization's policy first. Product settings do not override company rules. Think about third parties: customer, patient and colleague data belongs to people who did not consent to your use. Exam tip: When a scenario shows personal data and a restrictive policy, the best answer is to remove or anonymize the identifiers (or use an approved, covered setup) before using Claude. "Tell Claude not to keep it" or "it's only internal" does not satisfy the policy.

1.title: Privacy Controls in the Product
1.text: Privacy Controls in the Product. Model training (consumer plans). On Free, Pro and Max, chats may be used to improve models if you allow it (a Model Improvement setting under privacy settings), or if flagged for safety review; incognito chats are never used. Check the setting yourself. Commercial plans. Team, Enterprise and the A P I (application programming interface) are governed by commercial terms; Anthropic does not train on customer content from these by default. A data processing addendum and, for health data, a business associate agreement for eligible commercial customers are separate contracts.

1.title: Privacy Controls in the Product, continued
1.text: Privacy Controls in the Product, continued. Work versus personal accounts. Use the company-approved account for work data; do not use a personal account for company information. Incognito chat. Not saved to history or memory; but it is still subject to retention for safety (thirty days) and to company policy. Memory. Sensitive topics are off by default; some items are never saved; review and delete memory; Team and Enterprise owners cannot read individual memories.

1.title: Privacy Controls in the Product, continued
1.text: Privacy Controls in the Product, continued. Shared chats. Sharing creates a link anyone can open; attached files and raw tool data are not included; unshare in Settings; on Team and Enterprise sharing stays inside the organization. Artifacts. Private by default; check whether shared storage is used before entering sensitive information; do not run untrusted artifacts. Connectors. Claude sees only what you can access; keep connected sources narrow; approvals before sending or sharing; connector data is not used for training.

1.title: Privacy Controls in the Product, continued
1.text: Privacy Controls in the Product, continued. Files and code execution. Instructions hidden in untrusted files or sites (prompt injection) could try to make Claude leak conversation data; monitor actions; use files from trusted sources. Web search and fetch. Claude may use your approximate location; it reads public pages; do not paste confidential text into a search. Feedback. Thumbs up or down can store the whole conversation for review and analysis (up to five years, delinked from your I D).

1.title: Regulation and Everyday Use
1.text: Regulation and Everyday Use. Regulations (for example G D P R and similar privacy laws, H I P A A for health data, rules for payment card data, sector rules, A I laws) apply to how data about people is processed, no matter which tool you use. The associate's job is not to interpret law but to recognize when regulated data or a high-risk decision is involved, follow the organization's policy, and ask Legal, Privacy or Security when unsure. Be aware of data residency, retention and contract terms for the account you use; these differ between consumer and commercial plans and across cloud options.

2.title: Regulation and Everyday Use, continued
2.text: Regulation and Everyday Use, continued. A I-generated content marking: Claude outputs may carry invisible watermarks or content credentials; a mark is a signal, not proof, and a missing mark proves nothing. Keep a record of how A I was used on important work.

2.title: Regulation and Everyday Use, continued
2.text: Regulation and Everyday Use, continued. The figure shows this: Before sharing data with Claude: check purpose, classify the data, minimize or anonymize, use the approved tool and account, and ask Legal or Privacy when unsure. Exam tip: Sort every scenario into appropriate, allowed with controls, or not allowed, then check the data class before you share anything.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Three zones: Appropriate, allowed with controls and human review, not allowed. High-risk areas: Legal, medical, financial, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education, public benefits. Not allowed: Fraud, fake reviews, harassment, disinformation, unauthorized access, surveillance without consent. Data classes: Public, internal, confidential, regulated (P I I, P H I, payment, credentials). Rules: Minimize, anonymize or redact, never share secrets, policy first. Not a control: "Don't retain this" instruction, incognito alone, "it's internal". Accounts: Company-approved account for work data; commercial terms for business data. Sharing: Link equals anyone can view; unshare in Settings. Prompt injection: Untrusted files and sites can carry instructions; monitor. Regulation: Recognize, follow policy, ask Legal, Privacy or Security.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A store manager wants Claude to find the busiest delivery hours from an export of orders that lists each customer's full name, home address and phone number. Company policy restricts personal data in A I tools. What is the best action? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Removing the identifiers keeps the analysis possible and satisfies the policy; the other options either breach it or abandon the task unnecessarily.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which request should be refused or stopped? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Fake reviews are deceptive artificial activity and violate the Usage Policy.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. H R wants Claude to rank applicants and automatically reject the bottom half. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Employment is a high-risk area that needs a human decision-maker and disclosure.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A consultant uses a personal free account to analyze a client's confidential contract. What is the main concern? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Use the approved account and follow policy for confidential data.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. An employee puts a customer's home address into an incognito chat, thinking that makes it private. What is true? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Incognito is not an exemption from policy; chats are still retained for safety for a period.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Select two. Which two are good privacy habits when using Claude at work? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and C. Sharing only the data a task needs and redacting personal identifiers are the core privacy practices for everyday work with Claude.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. What does sharing a chat by link do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Shared chats are viewable by anyone with the link (on commercial plans, sharing stays within the organization).

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. A document from an unknown website contains hidden text telling Claude to send the conversation to a web address. What is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Untrusted files can contain instructions that try to misuse Claude.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Which statement about regulated data is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Users are not expected to interpret law; they recognize regulated data and high-risk decisions, follow policy and ask Legal or Privacy.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Which data class can usually be used freely in Claude? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Public information is low risk; the others need controls or must not be used.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: B. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: B. Question five: D. Question six: B and C. Question seven: C. Question eight: B. Question nine: A. Question ten: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
